Lyuboml New Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Liuboml, Ukraine

Demolished. Functioning by the 19th century and appearing on mid-19th-century Russian maps, this cemetery was fenced in 1930, then demolished by Soviet authorities in the 1970s-80s; up to seven postwar tombstones (1966-1970s) survived, though thick vegetation has since blocked confirmation. A mass grave of local Jews killed during WWII lies 150 meters west, marked by a memorial. Liuboml's Jewish community, first mentioned in 1370, is among the oldest in the former Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth; it survived the Khmelnytsky uprising and built a fortress-synagogue in 1670 that outlasted a 1728-29 fire. Population reached 3,297 (74%) by 1897; interwar Tarbut and Yavne schools served the community. German occupation from June 23, 1941 established a ghetto that December; residents formed underground armed groups producing false papers before the final mass execution of 1,000 Jews on October 1, 1942.
